intro: The most useful verb in English. Use it to say who you are, how you feel, where you are, how old you are and what the weather is like.
objectifs: Use “to be” in the present with every subject, in the full form and the short form.
Know when English uses “to be” where other languages use “have” (age, hunger, cold, fear).
Make simple sentences about yourself: name, job, feelings, place.

texte: “To be” is irregular. It has three forms in the present: am, is and are. Learn them by heart: you need them in almost every sentence.
We use the short form (contraction) when we speak and in messages. We use the full form in careful writing or to make something stronger.
sections.note: “You” is for one person and for many people. The verb is always “are”: you are.

texte: We use it to say who we are (name, nationality, job), how we feel, where we are, and to describe people and things.
exemples: Job: use a / an before a job.

texte: Many languages say “I have 30 years” or “I have hunger”. English uses “to be” + an adjective or a number. This is the most common mistake for beginners.
An English sentence always has a subject. When there is no person, use “it”: for time, weather, distance and situations.
Never say “Is late” or “Is raining”. Say “It's late”, “It's raining”.

formule: I am · you are · he / she / it is · we are · they are
prononciation: “I'm” sounds like /aɪm/: the word “time” without the t.
“you're” and “your” sound almost the same. “they're”, “their” and “there” all sound like /ðeə/.
In “he's” and “she's”, the s sounds like /z/. In “it's”, it sounds like /s/.
For “th” in “they”, put your tongue between your teeth and use your voice: /ð/. It is not a z or a d.
erreurs: Hunger, thirst, cold, fear: “to be” + adjective.
Use a / an before a job in the singular.
With they, we and you: always “are”.

dialogue.contexte: First day on a course. Two people meet.
lignes: Hi! I'm Anna. Are you new here?
Anna says her name and asks a question.
Yes, I am. I'm Karim. I'm from Douala.
Nice to meet you, Karim. Are you a student?
A polite phrase when you meet someone.
No, I'm not. I'm a nurse. And you?
“I'm a nurse”: a before the job.
I'm a teacher. Oh, it's nine o'clock. We're late!
Oh no! Let's go. I'm ready.

mots: a person who studies at a school or university
with a lot of things to do

exercices.consigne: Complete with am, is or are.
Each sentence has one mistake. Write it correctly.
Put the words in the right order to make a sentence.
Write four true sentences about you with “to be”: your name, your age, your job or studies, how you feel today.
items: I'm John. I'm 34. I'm an accountant. Today I'm a bit tired but happy.

a_retenir: I am · you are · he / she / it is · we are · they are. When you speak: I'm, you're, he's, she's, it's, we're, they're.
Age, hunger, thirst, cold, heat, fear, right, wrong: use “to be”.
Before a job: a / an (She's a nurse. He's an engineer.).
